source.title: Noise Injection Systemically Degrades Large Language Model Safety Guardrails
source.authors: Prithviraj Singh Shahani; Kaveh Eskandari Miandoab; Matthias Scheutz

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables and figures are rendered as flattened text, but the Appendix B mean values and standard deviations can be assigned to their models and noise levels.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether safety behavior is vulnerable to a different intervention—Gaussian noise added to activations—using harmful-output rates. It does not test the listed fine-tuning, token-position, prefix, suffix, or decoding claims directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-output rates under activation noise in Experiment A and rates for noise-tuned Gemma 2B at σ = 0.24 in Experiment C. Experiment B measures math accuracy under noise, not safety behavior. The discussion and related-work claims about harmful or benign fine-tuning are citations, not results of this study. No per-token KL, compliant prefill, suffix, decoding-change, parameter-localization, or safety-depth measurements are reported. To stay within the 60-row limit, Appendix B rows retain the zero-noise baseline and five of the six nonzero noise levels per model; the omitted first nonzero level for each model is listed in rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study injects Gaussian noise into all activation layers and measures harmful-output rates. That is a different intervention from every version. It is not fine-tuning (V1, V2), per-token KL (V3), or prefill, suffix or decoding changes (V4). It does not localize weights (V5) or train safety to reach deeper token positions (V7). Its talk of 'surface-level' safety and its Qi et al. figures are citations or interpretation. The reader's 'tests/T2' is wrong: no version is tested. Results belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add three points. The authors report noise raises harmful rates by up to ~30% (p<0.001) in most models. They attribute Qwen2.5's resilience to RL post-training, which they hypothesise but do not test. They argue from a math-only experiment (B) that deeper fine-tuning gives only marginal extra protection.
record.recipe_differences: The study injects Gaussian noise into activation layers at inference and during a noise-augmented fine-tuning defense; it does not use the original sources’ harmful/benign fine-tuning interventions or first-token KL/prefill methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful-output rates vary with noise scale and model: most tested models rise under noise, Qwen2.5 rises less, and Yi 1.5 declines at the reported noise levels. Noise-tuned Gemma 2B protection is strongest within the training range and drops outside it.

fits_no_version.finding: Gaussian activation noise raises judge-rated harmful-output rates in most safety-tuned open models. Qwen2.5 is more resilient; Yi 1.5 6B declines under noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety refusals in instruct models are brittle to untargeted activation noise, with strong model dependence.

fits_no_version.finding: Noise-augmented safety fine-tuning of Gemma 2B lowers attack success within the training noise range. It still yields 32% (Llama Guard) and 20% (GPT-OSS) at σ=0.24.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise-augmented safety training gives protection localized to the training noise range.

fits_no_version.finding: DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama 3.1 8B scores 71% harmful vs 1% for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct. The distill model is built from a different checkpoint, so this is not a controlled fine-tuning test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-distillation models may lack the refusal behaviour of their family's instruct models.

record.problems: Experiment A relies on automated judges; the paper notes they may misclassify incoherent text as harmful. Noise ranges were selected using an initial n = 1 trial, and Experiment C is limited to Gemma 2B. Several reported Appendix B significance comparisons are attached to a listed noise value that does not match the table header (for example Qwen 2); table means and standard deviations are recorded as printed.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B, Tables 2–10: omitted the first nonzero noise level for each of the nine models to meet the 60-row cap; retained the baseline and five higher noise levels per model. No Experiment B math-accuracy rows were included because they do not measure safety behavior. Experiment C’s other curve values are figure-only and were not separately extracted; the text gives the two judge-specific rates at σ = 0.24.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning; only Qi et al. is cited.
Benign fine-tuning effect on harmful compliance. Experiment B fine-tunes on GSM8K but measures math accuracy only, not safety.
Prefilled compliant starts, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes.
Localization of safety in few weights or ranks; prior work is cited only.
Data or objective as cause of token-level shallowness. The authors speculate about SFT vs RL (Qwen2.5) without a controlled test.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens. Noise-augmented training targets activation noise, not token depth.

missing.what: No-noise harmful rates for Mistral 7B Instruct (70%) and DeepSeek-R1-distilled Llama 3.1 8B (71%)
missing.versions: none (DeepSeek distill loosely near V2 but confounded)

missing.what: Base Gemma 2B vs noise-tuned attack success curves σ=0–0.32 (figure only)

record.verdict_notes: Several printed baseline-comparison statistics in Appendix B do not match the table means. They also reference σ values absent from the tables (Gemma-2 9B σ=1.0, Qwen2 σ=0.003). Noise ranges were chosen per model from n=1 pilot runs so as to produce significant change, which inflates apparent effects. Judges may score incoherent text as harmful. The abstract's 'deeper safety fine-tuning' claim rests on GSM8K accuracy, not safety.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and whether a few to a few hundred examples remove refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence and its distribution over response positions.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes; activation noise is a different intervention.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether the data or objective that creates safety causes token-level shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens; the study tests noise-augmented training against activation noise, not token-depth.
